title: ODC ‐Driven Polyamines Synthesis Sustains the Self‐Renewal of Glioblastoma Stem Cells and Drives Tumor Aggressiveness

sections.abstract: Glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) are crucial drivers of tumor progression and therapeutic resistance in glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), yet the molecular mechanisms maintaining their self‐renewal remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a critical role for polyamine metabolism in GSCs maintenance. We show that GSCs exhibit elevated polyamine levels compared to non‐stem tumor cells, attributed to enhanced ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) expression. High ODC expression correlates with poor patient prognosis in GBM. Genetic and pharmacologic targeting of ODC attenuated GSCs self‐renewal and tumorigenicity. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized metabolic dependency of GSCs on polyamine synthesis, and ODC may be a potential therapeutic target in GBM.
sections.introduction:
GBM is the most aggressive and prevalent form of primary malignant brain tumor, with a grim prognosis and a median survival time of approximately 14 months despite multimodal treatment strategies [ 1 , 2 ]. The poor prognosis is largely attributed to a subpopulation of GSCs, which drive tumor initiation, therapeutic resistance, and recurrence through their capacity for self‐renewal and multilineage differentiation [ 3 , 4 ]. Therefore, understanding the molecular mechanisms that maintain GSCs self‐renewal is crucial for developing more effective therapeutic strategies.

Polyamines (putrescine, spermidine, and spermine) are positively charged small molecules that modulate critical cellular processes, including transcription, translation, and chromatin stability, through dynamic interactions with nucleic acids and proteins [ 5 , 6 ]. As the rate‐limiting enzyme in polyamine biosynthesis, ODC catalyzes the de‐carboxylation of ornithine to generate putrescine, the foundational precursor for higher‐order polyamines [ 7 , 8 ]. Notably, ODC activity is directly governed by oncogenic drivers such as MYC [ 9 ], positioning it as a pivotal metabolic nexus in malignancy. Clinical correlative studies have consistently revealed ODC overexpression as an independent prognostic marker for poor outcomes in colorectal carcinoma, breast cancer, and other solid tumors, where pharmacological or genetic ODC suppression triggers apoptosis and curbs metastatic dissemination [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ]. This positions ODC as a metabolic linchpin connecting oncogenic signaling to tumor progression.

Despite these advances, the functional landscape of ODC in GSCs remains uncharted. Mounting evidence suggests that metabolic reprogramming sustains GSCs stemness [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ]. Intriguingly, polyamines have recently emerged as dual regulators of both oxidative stress adaptation and chromatin remodeling [ 22 , 23 ], yet their spatial–temporal dynamics in GSCs maintenance remain enigmatic. This knowledge gap is particularly critical given the blood–brain barrier's restriction of conventional ODC inhibitors (α‐difluoromethylornithine, DFMO) and the unique metabolic dependencies reported in neural stem cell niches [ 24 ]. Gene editing techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9 provide more precise tools for directly targeting ODC, avoiding off‐target drug effects and revealing the molecular consequences of polyamine depletion [ 25 , 26 , 27 ].

Here, through comparative metabolomics profiling of matched GSCs and NSTCs, we identify GSCs as major sources of polyamines in GBM. We demonstrate that elevated ODC expression drives polyamine synthesis in GSCs and correlates with poor patient prognosis. Our findings uncover a previously unrecognized metabolic vulnerability in GSCs and suggest that targeting ODC may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for GBM.
sections.methods:
All patient‐derived GSCs were gifted from Dr. Jeremy Rich (University of Pittsburgh, USA) and Dr. Jennifer S. Yu (Cleveland Clinic, USA) and were maintained in the Neurobasal Medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) supplemented with B‐27 supplement without putrescine (Yeasen Biotechnology, China), sodium pyruvate, L‐glutamine, Penicillin–Streptomycin, EGF, and bFGF (10 ng/mL each, R&D Systems, USA). These assessed cells were used for sphere‐forming, in vitro limiting dilution assay, and orthotopic mouse xenografts in immunocompromised mice. GSCs were cultured in DMEM with 10% FBS for 7 days to differentiate into NSTCs.

All GBM tumor samples and adjacent normal brain tissues were obtained from the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) General Hospital (Beijing, China). All tissue acquisitions are conducted with informed consent from patients. All procedures are approved with the Ethical Committee of the PLA General Hospital requirements.

Collect 10 7 cells and dissolve them in 100 μL methanol. Subject the sample to repeated freeze–thaw cycles (three times) to completely release cellular contents, with the precipitate used for protein quantification. Dry the sample using a freeze vacuum dryer, then reconstitute it with 20 μL methanol for subsequent mass spectrometry detection.

Non‐targeted metabolomics analysis was performed with a Vanquish HPLC and a Q Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) interfaced with an electrospray ionization source. The mass spectrometer was operated in both positive and negative ion modes with IDA experiments (Information Dependent Acquisition). The resulting mass spectra were exported into Progenesis QI software for further processing and annotated metabolic features by using a combination of a self‐built library and public libraries (HMDB, KEGG).

Targeted polyamine mass spectrometry was performed with a UPLC I‐Class HPLC and a XEVO TQ‐S Micro mass spectrometer (Waters Corporation, USA) interfaced with an electrospray ionization source. The peak areas were calculated using the TargetLynx software, and the quantitative results were obtained by the single‐point isotope internal standard method.

Whole cell lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer (Biosharp Life Science, China) with protease and phosphatase inhibitor (Roche, Switzerland). Protein concentration was determined by Bradford Dye Reagent (Bio‐Rad, USA), and equal amounts of protein samples were resolved by SDS‐PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes (Merck Millipore, Germany). TBST with 5% skim milk was used for blocking. Blots were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C, followed by HRP‐conjugated secondary antibodies (1:5000, Jakson, USA) for 1 h at room temperature. All antibody information is provided in Table S1 .

Tumor and NAT tissue samples from patients or xenograft samples were preserved in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, and then cut into 4 μm sections. After deparaffinization and dehydration, tissue sections were incubated in 3% H 2 O 2 for 10 min, blocked with 3% BSA and 0.5% Triton X‐100 in PBS for 1 h at room temperature, and the slides were treated with primary antibodies at 4°C overnight. Secondary antibodies were added and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. DAB staining was used to detect specific molecules, and the slides were counterstained with hematoxylin.

The immunostaining was carried out overnight at 4°C, followed by incubation with fluorochrome‐conjugated antibodies. Finally, DAPI was used to stain the cell nuclei. Images were acquired using a ZEISS LSM 880 (Zeiss, Germany) confocal microscope. All antibody information is provided in Table S1 .

Construct a lentiviral vector containing guide RNA targeting ODC, and package it in HEK293T cells using psPAX2 and pMD‐VSVG. Luciferase‐expressing GSCs were first transduced with lentivirus and treated with 10 μg/mL Blasticidin (Beyotime Biotechnology, China). The Blasticidin‐resistant cells were then transduced with lentivirus containing guide RNAs against ODC. Stably transfected monoclonal cell lines were selected with 2 μg/mL puromycin (Beyotime Biotechnology, China). Knockout cells were analyzed by IB. The guide RNA information is provided in Table S2 .

4 × 10 3 GSCs were plated on the 96 well plates. Cell viability was measured using the CellTiter‐Glo (Promega, USA) assay on the 0, 2nd, 4th, and 6th days. Data was normalized to Day 0. The data presented are from three replicates.

4 × 10 3 GSCs were plated on the 96 well plates. A fluorescence microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) was used to count sphere numbers on the 5th day. Each group has three replicates.

Female BALB/c nude mice, aged 4–6 weeks, were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co. Ltd. (Beijing, China). All mice used in this study were maintained in the pathogen‐free barrier animal facility at the National Center of Biomedical Analysis. For the intracranial tumor xenograft model, sgNT or sgODC treated luciferase stably GSC were intracranially injected into the right frontal lobes of BALB/c nude mice at a concentration of 5 × 10 4 cells using a stereotaxic instrument. Mice were imaged using the Xenogen IVIS (PerkinElmer, USA) to determine tumor incidence and tumor size at specified time points. The animals were imaged weekly until they exhibited typical neurological symptoms, and then euthanized. Brains were collected for Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) or immunohistochemistry staining.

For subcutaneous tumor xenograft model, 5 × 10 5 GSCs are injected into the right flank of nude mice. Tumor size was measured every 3 days until 18–20 days post‐inoculation; the mice are euthanized and harvested the tumor.

The dataset GSE54791 was obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/ ). Processed tumor gene expression and clinical data for TCGA ( https://www.cancer.gov/tcga ), CGGA, Rembrandt, Gravendeel, FREIJE, and JOO cohorts have been obtained from the GlioVis portal ( http://recur.bioinfo.cnio.es ). All datasets mentioned are derived from online public databases.

GraphPad Prism 8 (GraphPad Software Inc., USA) was used for all statistical analyses. All grouped data are presented as mean ± SD unless otherwise specified and repeated at least three times. Statistical significance was evaluated using either Student's t ‐test or one‐way and two‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for multiple comparisons. Survival rates were calculated utilizing the Kaplan–Meier technique, and variations in mortality were assessed through the log‐rank test. Significance was determined for all tests with p values < 0.05 considered significant.
sections.results:
To identify metabolites influencing the self‐renewal of GSCs, we conducted an untargeted intracellular metabolic analysis of four patient‐derived GSC lines and their paired NSTCs, which had differentiated from each respective GSC line. Metabolite enrichment analysis revealed that pathways related to spermidine and spermine biosynthesis were most significantly enriched in GSCs compared to NSTCs (Figure 1A ). Putrescine and spermidine, key intermediates in the polyamine metabolic pathway, showed notably higher levels in all four GSC lines (Figure 1B ). To confirm these observations, we used targeted mass spectrometry to measure spermidine, its precursor putrescine, and its downstream product spermine. As shown in Figure 1C , GSCs had significantly increased levels of all three polyamines relative to NSTCs.

Compared to NSTCs, polyamines are highly expressed in GSCs. (A) Enrichment analysis of metabolites with significant differences between GSCs and NSTCs. (B) Heatmap of mass spectrometry analysis of intracellular metabolites from four types of GSCs and paired NSTCs. Red indicates upregulated metabolites, while blue indicates downregulated ones. (C) Polyamines content in GSCs and paired NSTCs by mass spectrometry in vitro. Data were represented as mean ± SD. p values were obtained by unpaired t test with Welch's correction (C). * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.005, *** p < 0.0005.

In mammalian cells, three key enzymes—ornithine decarboxylase (ODC), spermidine synthase (SRM), and spermine synthase (SMS)—are essential for polyamine metabolism (Figure 2A ). ODC, the rate‐limiting enzyme, converts ornithine to putrescine, which is then converted to spermidine by SRM, and subsequently to spermine by SMS [ 28 ]. To determine which enzyme(s) were responsible for the heightened polyamine levels in GSCs, we performed immunoblot (IB) analyses on the four GSC lines and their NSTC counterparts. We found that ODC was significantly upregulated in GSCs, whereas levels of SRM, SMS, and the polyamine transporter SLC3A2 remained unchanged (Figure 2B ). Further examination in GSC‐derived subcutaneous tumors sorted with CD133 magnetic beads showed that ODC expression was also significantly elevated in CD133+ cells (Figure 2C ), suggesting that enhanced ODC activity underlies increased polyamine levels in GSCs.

ODC is highly expressed in GSCs compared to NSTCs. (A) Metabolic pathway of polyamines. Metabolic enzymes are in red. (B) Protein levels of ODC, SLC3A2, SRM, SMS in GSCs and paired NSTCs. (C) Protein levels of ODC in CD133 positive or negative GSCs. (D) Expression levels of ODC1 between TPCs and DGCs in the GEO dataset. Data were represented as mean ± SD. p values were obtained by unpaired t test with Welch's correction (D).

Consistently, analysis of a GBM patient dataset from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO: GSE54791 ) showed that ODC1 (the gene encoding ODC) was significantly upregulated in patient‐derived stem‐like tumor‐propagating cells (TPCs) compared with differentiated glioblastoma cells (DGCs) (Figure 2D ). These data strongly support that the elevated ODC expression is GSC‐specific.

To investigate the functional role of ODC in GSCs, we generated ODC‐knockout cell lines using the CRISPR‐Cas9 system with specific sgRNAs in two independent GSC models. Immunoblotting confirmed efficient ODC ablation (Figure 3A ), and targeted mass spectrometry revealed that ODC deletion significantly reduced intracellular levels of putrescine, spermidine, and spermine (Figure 3B ). To exclude confounding effects of exogenous polyamines, a customized putrescine‐free B‐27 supplement was utilized, with mass spectrometry confirming the absence of residual polyamines in the culture system (Figure S1A ). Cell proliferation assays (Figure 3C ) and Ki67 flow cytometry (Figure S1B ) demonstrated that ODC knockout markedly impaired GSCs proliferation and viability. Similarly, treatment with the ODC inhibitor Eflornithine (DFMO) significantly reduced GSCs proliferation (Figure 3D ). In contrast, ODC depletion did not affect the growth of NSTCs (Figure S1C,D ), likely attributable to the lower baseline ODC expression in NSTCs. These findings indicate that ODC sustains GSCs proliferation by regulating polyamines metabolism.

Polyamines are crucial for the proliferation of GSCs. (A) IB analysis of ODC expression in 387 and 3832 GSCs transduced with sgNT or sgODC. (B) Polyamines content in 387 and 3832 GSCs transduced with sgNT or sgODC by mass spectrometry in vitro. (C) Growth curves of 387 and 3832 GSCs expressing sgNT or sgODC. (D) Growth curves of 387 and 3832 GSCs treated with an increasing dose of DFMO. Data were represented as mean ± SD. p values were obtained by ordinary one‐way ANOVA (B) and two‐way ANOVA multiple comparison (C, D). * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.005, *** p < 0.0005.

Given the robust self‐renewal capacity of GSCs, we further evaluated the impact of ODC depletion using sphere formation assays (Figure 4A ) and limiting dilution assays (Figure 4B ). The results revealed that ODC knockout significantly reduced both the number of GSC‐derived spheres and their self‐renewal potential. Furthermore, treatment with the ODC inhibitor eflornithine (DFMO) markedly suppressed GSCs sphere‐forming ability (Figure 4C ). Collectively, these data demonstrate that ODC is essential for maintaining GSCs self‐renewal through the regulation of polyamine metabolism.

Polyamines are crucial for the self‐renewal of GSCs. (A) Representative images and quantification of the neurospheres derived from 387 and 3832 GSCs expressing sgNT or sgODC; Scale bar, 50 μm. (B) In vitro extreme limiting dilution assays of 387 and 3832 GSCs expressing sgNT or sgODC. (C) Representative images and quantification of the neurospheres derived from 387 and 3832 GSCs treated with an increasing dose of DFMO; Scale bar, 50 μm.

We next investigated whether polyamines produced by GSCs influence their tumorigenic potential in vivo. To do so, GSCs stably expressing firefly luciferase were transduced with either a non‐targeting control (sgNT) or an ODC‐targeting guide (sgODC), then orthotopically implanted into BALB/c nude mice (Figure 5A and Figure S2A ). GSCs transduced with sgNT formed brain tumors approximately 20 days post‐injection, at which point animals were monitored for weight loss and neurological signs and euthanized when these appeared. Bioluminescence imaging (BLI) and survival analysis showed that ODC knockout markedly inhibited glioma growth in vivo (Figure 5B,C and Figure S2B,C ). Kaplan–Meier survival curves indicated that mice receiving sgODC GSCs exhibited a median survival that was extended by more than 4 weeks compared to controls (Figure 5D and Figure S2D ). Histological examination (H&E staining) confirmed that tumors arising from sgODC GSCs were significantly smaller than those from sgNT GSCs (Figure 5E and Figure S2E ). These data collectively demonstrate that ODC and polyamine metabolism drive GBM progression.

Highly expressed ODC promotes GSCs malignant progression. (A) Representative immunohistochemistry images of ODC expression measured on mice with 387 GSCs expressing sgNT or sgODC xenograft tumors. Upper scale bars, 100 μm; lower scale bars, 50 μm. (B) Representative bioluminescence images of intracranial tumor growth in mice bearing GBM xenograft derived from luciferase‐labeled 387 GSCs expressing sgNT or sgODC ( n = 10 mice per group). Time points indicate days after intracranial injection of GSCs. (C) Quantification of intracranial tumor growth in mice bearing GBM xenograft derived from luciferase‐labeled 387 GSCs expressing sgNT or sgODC ( n = 10 mice per group). (D) Survival curves of mice bearing intracranial patient‐derived 387 xenograft expressing sgNT or sgODC ( n = 10 mice per group). (E) Representative images of H&E stained sections of mouse brains collected when mice bearing control 387 GSC cells exhibited neurological signs. Scale bars, 2 mm. Data were represented as mean ± SD. p values were obtained by two‐way ANOVA multiple comparison (C) and log‐rank test (D). *** p < 0.0005.

ODC has been previously shown to be overexpressed in diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) and implicated in tumor progression [ 29 ], and is considered a potential biomarker in various adult cancers [ 12 , 13 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ]. To assess ODC expression and its clinical relevance in GBM, we analyzed data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA, HG‐U133A), the Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA), and other glioma datasets. These analyses revealed that ODC mRNA is highly upregulated in GBM compared with non‐tumor brain tissues (Figure 6A ). Across four different datasets, ODC expression correlated positively with increasing glioma malignancy (Figure 6B and Figure S3A ). Kaplan–Meier survival curves demonstrated that patients with lower ODC expression experienced longer overall survival (OS) than those with higher expression (Figure 6C and Figure S3B ).

ODC is associated with GBM progression and patient survival. (A) Comparison of ODC1 mRNA levels (TPM, transcripts per million) in tumors and matched normal tissues from GBM patients in the TCGA‐GBM dataset. For the boxplots, the center lines mark the median, the box limits indicate the 25% and 75%, and the whiskers extend 1.5× the interquartile range from the 25% and 75% (biologically independent samples n = 10 for normal, n = 528 for tumor). (B) Comparison of ODC1 mRNA levels (TPM) in different stages of tumor from human GBM patients in the TCGA‐GBMLGG, CGGA, Gravendeel, and Rembrandt dataset. (C) Kaplan–Meier overall survival analysis of ODC1 for GBM patients from the CGGA, FREIJE, and JOO dataset. Using optimal cutoff, p value was calculated using the two‐side log‐rank test. (D) Representative immunohistochemistry images and evaluation of ODC expression measured on a microarray that contains grade 1 ( n = 17), grade 2 ( n = 45), grade 3 ( n = 19) and grade 4 ( n = 20) glioma tissue. Upper scale bars, 100 μm; lower scale bars, 50 μm. (E) Analysis of ODC expression and the progression‐free survival of 159 glioma patients (ODC high, n = 99; ODC low, n = 60). (F) Representative immunohistochemistry images and quantification of ODC expression for human GBM samples; scale bars, 20 μm. Data were represented as mean ± SD. p values were obtained by unpaired two‐tailed Student's t ‐test (A) and two‐side log‐rank test (C).

To corroborate these findings, we conducted immunohistochemistry (IHC) on a glioma tissue microarray (HBraG159Su01). ODC staining intensity was significantly greater in high‐grade gliomas relative to low‐grade gliomas (Figure 6D ), and higher ODC IHC scores were associated with reduced patient survival (Figure 6E ). Collectively, these results indicate that elevated ODC expression is an adverse prognostic factor in GBM.

Finally, to explore the relationship between ODC and human GBM, we analyzed tumor and adjacent normal tissues (NATs) from patients with high‐grade gliomas (Figure S3C ). ODC was significantly upregulated in GBM samples compared to NATs (Figure 6F ). Together, these data highlight a strong association between ODC and GBM.
sections.discussion:
In this study, we unveil a pivotal role of GSCs in polyamine metabolism in GBM. Although elevated polyamines levels in GBM are well‐documented [ 34 , 35 ], underscoring their importance in tumor proliferation, therapy resistance, and macrophage M2 polarization [ 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 ], the precise source of these polyamines has remained elusive. Here, we demonstrate that GSCs serve as the principal sources of polyamines, driven by the overexpression of the rate‐limiting enzyme ODC. ODC inhibition in GSCs resulted in markedly reduced tumorigenicity and self‐renewal, suggesting the potential for therapeutic interventions targeting polyamines biosynthesis in these cells. Notably, previous studies indicate that simultaneous blockade of both polyamines synthesis and uptake may produce superior therapeutic outcomes compared with either approach alone [ 29 ]. While our current work focuses on limiting polyamines synthesis in GSCs, future efforts exploring polyamines uptake inhibitors in conjunction with this strategy could enhance treatment efficacy, particularly in recurrent or refractory GBM.

Our findings align with prior reports demonstrating anti‐glioma efficacy of the ODC inhibitor DFMO but reveal a critical divergence: CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated ODC knockout elicits superior suppression of GSCs proliferation, suggesting that complete enzymatic ablation disrupts compensatory polyamine salvage pathways, such as transmembrane uptake upregulation, that likely undermine pharmacologic ODC inhibition [ 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 ]. This genetic rigor resolves a long‐debated limitation of polyamine‐targeted therapies, where residual ODC activity or microenvironmental polyamine scavenging sustains tumor resilience [ 44 , 45 ].

While our in vitro models robustly validate ODC as a therapeutic target, clinical translation faces dual barriers. First, achieving in vivo specificity: GSCs reside within a neurologically privileged niche [ 46 ], necessitating advanced delivery platforms (e.g., tumor‐penetrating nanoparticles or BBB‐crossing AAVs) to spatially restrict ODC knockout while sparing normal neural progenitors dependent on polyamines for neurogenesis. Second, mitigating systemic toxicity: Conditional knockout systems (e.g., Cre‐LoxP with GSC‐specific promoters like PROM1/CD133) or polyamines depletion responsive “synthetic rescue” circuits could balance efficacy and safety, a strategy gaining traction in CRISPR therapeutics [ 26 ]. Combinatorial approaches, such as coupling ODC suppression with radiotherapy to exploit polyamine‐depleted redox vulnerability, may further circumvent resistance by simultaneously targeting proliferative bulk tumors and quiescent GSCs.

We acknowledge the perspective that our models, while valuable, utilize purified GSCs. Crucially, our intracranial xenografts, initiated with GSCs, recapitulate intratumoral heterogeneity as engrafted GSCs differentiate in vivo, generating progeny expressing NSTC markers alongside persistent GSCs. Thus, the resulting tumors represent dynamic mixed populations. The significant therapeutic efficacy of ODC knockdown in these models (Figure 5 and Figure S2 )—tumor growth inhibition and prolonged survival—demonstrates impact on both initiating GSCs and derived NSTCs within the evolving tumor mass. However, we recognize these immunocompromised xenografts lack the full human GBM TME complexity, including its immune components. Furthermore, while our findings elucidate the importance of ODC in GSC maintenance, this study does not encompass the immunomodulatory functions of ODC within the GBM microenvironment. Recent work reveals that polyamine blockade reprograms myeloid‐derived suppressor cell (MDSC) metabolism, potentiating checkpoint inhibitor responses [ 47 ]. Whether ODC knockout alters immunogenic signaling (e.g., MHC‐I presentation) or cytokine secretion in GSCs remains an open question with therapeutic implications. Therefore, utilizing patient‐derived organoids (PDOs), which better preserve native architecture, cellular heterogeneity, and critical TME elements, is a vital next step. We are actively establishing GBM PDOs and commit to evaluating ODC inhibition in these more physiologically relevant models in future work; additionally, employing syngeneic orthotopic models with intact immune systems or patient‐derived organoid‐immune cocultures will be critical to specifically clarify the immunomodulatory roles of ODC targeting and its interactions within the complex TME.

By integrating genetic ODC ablation with multiomic profiling, we redefine polyamine metabolism as a linchpin of GSCs self‐renewal, a dependency exploitable through precision gene editing. While technical hurdles persist, emerging CRISPR delivery technologies and combinatorial regimens position ODC targeting as a viable strategy against glioblastoma therapeutic recalcitrance. Crucially, our work underscores the necessity of moving beyond bulk tumor analyses to dissect metabolic heterogeneity within stem‐like subpopulations, a paradigm shift essential for overcoming the adaptive resilience of cancer [ 48 ].

In summary, our findings delineate a novel regulatory network that integrates metabolic and GSCs self‐renewal in GBM. By integrating genetic ODC ablation with multiomic profiling, we redefine polyamine metabolism as a linchpin of GSCs self‐renewal, a dependency exploitable through precision gene editing. While technical hurdles persist, emerging CRISPR delivery technologies and combinatorial regimens position ODC targeting as a viable strategy against glioblastoma therapeutic recalcitrance. Further in‐depth exploration of this strategy may pave the way for more effective interventions, ultimately offering renewed hope to patients afflicted by this devastating disease.
